attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter. He cites unnamed sources but makes the allegation himself.

semantics.note: Keeps the five companies, 'everything in their power', 'obfuscate' and the sourcing qualifier. It is correctly treated as a past observation about how the companies handled disclosure.

contract.note: The plain reading (deliberate, systematic hiding of AI operating costs, checked company by company) is ordinary and fair. Whether 'obfuscate' means leaving costs out or actively misleading, and how much intent must be shown, decides the result.

evidence.note: Stanford HAI index (Dec 2025) finds low and uneven transparency about foundation models. It does not measure cost disclosure by these five firms and does not show intent.
Microsoft's own disclosure of total capex and AI-related margin pressure. It is lumped-together reporting that neither proves nor rules out deliberate hiding of AI costs.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet shows a deliberate effort by each named company to hide AI costs. Nothing shows candid, complete cost disclosure that would rule it out either. Low transparency scores and combined capex figures cannot tell intent apart from ordinary confidentiality. The unnamed sources cannot be checked.

contract.note: Requiring a completed new round that was actually needed matches 'have to raise'. The scored core is the financing, and the hedged valuation scenarios are not treated as thresholds. Fair.

evidence.note: CNBC report (23 Oct 2026) that the CFO said OpenAI will list in 2027 confirms the delay premise. It also says a roughly $30B round was not yet signed and was framed as 'opportunistic'. That bears on the premise, not on the outcome.
Reuters-based report of a possible round valuing OpenAI above $1.4T. It describes fundraising in progress, not a completed financing.

reviews.rationale: The 2027 IPO timetable is confirmed by a reported CFO statement. By the cutoff no new private round had closed, so the early-resolution rule is not met. That a round was needed is not established (it was reportedly called 'opportunistic'), and there are no IPO terms to judge investor returns.

contract.note: Scoring the firm compute-pullback core after a real business failure, and treating the 'likely' parts as hedged, is a fair and ordinary reading. No deadline is imposed.
